subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 1! In this unit you will become confident with numbers of every size – from large whole numbers in the millions all the way down to tiny decimals in the thousandths. You will read them, write them, compare them, take them apart, scale them up and down, and round them. These are the numbers that run the real world. When Hassan checks that the water tanker holds 12,500 litres, when a scientist measures a butterfly wingspan of 0.375 inches, or when Amina counts out shillings at the Hargeisa market, they are all working with place value.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Read, write and understand whole numbers up to the millions, and decimals with up to three decimal places (tenths, hundredths, thousandths).
Explain the value of each digit in a number using its place.
Compose numbers by combining place value parts, and decompose numbers into their parts.
Regroup a decimal in different ways while keeping the same value.
Compare and order decimal numbers using place value.
Multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000, explaining how the digits move.
Round decimals to the nearest whole number, tenth, hundredth or thousandth.
Read and order negative numbers on a number line and in real contexts such as temperature.
Use estimation to check that answers are sensible, and apply these skills to money, measurement and science problems.
Describe how the place-value number system we use today developed, including the roles of ancient number systems such as Roman numerals and the Hindu-Arabic invention of zero and place value.
Estimate where a number lies on a number line that is only marked at its ends, such as a line from 0 to 10,000, using benchmark fractions like halves, quarters and tenths.

concepts.title: Place Value with Whole Numbers and Decimals
concepts.explanation:
Place value tells us what each digit in a number represents, based on its position. You already know this for whole numbers. In 352,714 the 3 means three hundred thousand, the 5 means fifty thousand, and so on. Each place to the left is ten times larger than the place to its right. Reading from the right, the whole-number places are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands and millions.

Decimals continue this same pattern in the other direction. When we move right past the decimal point, each place is ten times smaller than the one before it: tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. Let us look closely at the number 13.136:

The 1 is in the tens place, worth 10.

The 3 is in the ones place, worth 3.

The first 1 after the point is in the tenths place, worth 0.1.

The next 3 is in the hundredths place, worth 0.03.

The final 6 is in the thousandths place, worth 0.006.

Add the parts together and you get the whole number back: 10 + 3 + 0.1 + 0.03 + 0.006 = 13.136. This is the heart of place value – a number is just the sum of what each of its digits is worth.

A place value grid helps you see this clearly. Imagine columns labelled Tens, Ones, then the decimal point, then Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths. Writing 13.136 into the grid puts a 1 under Tens, a 3 under Ones, a 1 under Tenths, a 3 under Hundredths, and a 6 under Thousandths. Whenever you feel unsure about a decimal, draw this grid and place each digit in its column. It never lies to you.

Here is the most important warning of the whole unit: 0.3 is not the same as 0.03. In 0.3 the 3 sits in the tenths place, so it means 3 tenths, which is the same as 30 hundredths. In 0.03 the 3 sits in the hundredths place, so it means only 3 hundredths – ten times smaller. And 0.003 is smaller still. The digit 3 looks the same each time, but its place completely changes its value. This is exactly like whole numbers, where the 3 in 30 is very different from the 3 in 300.
concepts.example: One more helpful idea: adding a zero at the end of a decimal does not change its value. 0.3, 0.30 and 0.300 are all equal, because the extra zeros sit in empty places to the right and add nothing. This is very different from a whole number, where a zero on the end (turning 3 into 30) makes it ten times bigger. Understanding when a zero matters and when it does not is a sign of real place value confidence.

concepts.title: Reading and Writing Decimal Numbers
concepts.explanation:
There are two good ways to read a decimal aloud, and you should be comfortable with both. The first way simply reads the digits after the point one at a time. So 13.136 is read as “thirteen point one three six.” Notice we do not say “thirteen point one hundred and thirty-six” – after the point, we name each digit separately.

The second way uses the name of the last place. Because the smallest digit in 13.136 sits in the thousandths place, we can read it as “thirteen and one hundred thirty-six thousandths.” The word and stands for the decimal point. In the same way, 0.375 can be read as “zero point three seven five” or as “three hundred seventy-five thousandths.”

Writing a decimal from words works in reverse. Take “seven and twenty-four thousandths.” The word and marks the decimal point, so the whole part is 7. “Twenty-four thousandths” means 24 in the last three decimal places, which must be filled right up to the thousandths column. Twenty-four is 0-2-4 across the tenths, hundredths and thousandths, so we write 7.024. That leading zero in the tenths place is essential – without it we would have written 7.24, which is nearly ten times larger.
concepts.example: This is where many learners slip. When someone says “forty-three thousandths,” it is tempting to write 0.43, but that is forty-three hundredths. Forty-three thousandths must reach all the way to the thousandths column, so it is 0.043. Always ask yourself: which is the last place named? Then fill the digits so they end exactly in that column, using zeros as placeholders where needed.

concepts.title: Composing and Decomposing Numbers
concepts.explanation:
Composing means putting parts together to make a whole number. Decomposing means breaking a number into its parts. These are two sides of the same skill, and they prove that you truly understand what a number is made of.

The most natural way to decompose is by place value. For example, 2.139 breaks apart as 2 + 0.1 + 0.03 + 0.009, which we can say aloud as “2 ones + 1 tenth + 3 hundredths + 9 thousandths.” This is called expanded form. Try it with 8.146: the parts are 8 ones, 1 tenth, 4 hundredths and 6 thousandths, so 8.146 = 8 + 0.1 + 0.04 + 0.006.

But a number can be split in many different ways, not just by single place values. This is called regrouping, and it keeps the same value while showing it differently. Look at 0.546. We can write it as 0.5 + 0.04 + 0.006, but we can also write it as 0.4 + 0.146 – here we have kept 0.4 and gathered everything else into 0.146. Both versions still equal 0.546. Likewise 0.789 = 0.7 + 0.089. Being flexible like this is very useful later when you add, subtract and round.
concepts.example: A good check is to add your parts back together and see if you return to the original number. If you decompose 5.724 as 5.7 + 0.024, add them: 5.7 + 0.024 = 5.724. It matches, so your decomposition is correct. Money is a friendly way to picture this: think of 3.456 as 3 whole coins, 4 tenths, 5 hundredths and 6 thousandths, just as money splits into dollars, dimes, pennies and tiny fractions of a penny.

concepts.title: Comparing and Ordering Decimals
concepts.explanation:
To compare two decimals, work from left to right, one place at a time, and stop as soon as the digits differ. Start with the whole-number part; if those are equal, move to the tenths, then the hundredths, then the thousandths.

Compare 0.67 and 0.607. The whole parts are both 0. The tenths are both 6. Now the hundredths: 0.67 has 7 hundredths while 0.607 has 0 hundredths. Since 7 is more than 0, 0.67 > 0.607. A powerful trick is to give the numbers the same number of decimal places by adding zeros: 0.67 becomes 0.670, and now 0.670 against 0.607 is easy to see.

This is why the biggest myth in decimals – “more digits means a bigger number” – is false. The number 0.607 has more digits than 0.67, yet it is smaller. Length does not decide size; place value does. Always line up the decimal points and compare place by place.
concepts.example: To order a list of decimals, use the same method repeatedly. Take 0.67, 0.607, 0.7, 0.067. Rewrite them all with three decimal places: 0.670, 0.607, 0.700, 0.067. Now compare: the smallest is 0.067, then 0.607, then 0.670, then 0.700. So from smallest to largest the order is 0.067 < 0.607 < 0.67 < 0.7. Writing the extra zeros makes ordering almost automatic.

concepts.title: Multiplying and Dividing by 10, 100 and 1000
concepts.explanation:
When we multiply or divide by 10, 100 or 1000, the digits move to new places while keeping the same value – it only looks as though the decimal point has moved. Getting this picture right is the key to the whole idea.

When you multiply by a power of ten, the number gets larger, so the digits move to the LEFT:

72 × 10 = 720 – digits move 1 place left.

1.28 × 10 = 12.8 – digits move 1 place left.

0.85 × 100 = 85 – digits move 2 places left.

4.56 × 1000 = 4560 – digits move 3 places left.

When you divide by a power of ten, the number gets smaller, so the digits move to the RIGHT:

670 ÷ 100 = 6.7 – digits move 2 places right.

55 ÷ 10 = 5.5 – digits move 1 place right.

151 ÷ 1000 = 0.151 – digits move 3 places right.

The number of zeros tells you how many places to move: 10 has one zero (move 1 place), 100 has two zeros (move 2 places), 1000 has three zeros (move 3 places). A simple memory trick keeps the direction straight: Multiply = digits move Left = number gets Larger; Divide = digits move Right = number gets smalleR.

Sometimes you must add zeros as placeholders. For 0.85 × 100, moving the digits two places left turns 0.85 into 85. For 3 × 100 the digits move to give 300 – the two zeros hold the empty ones and tens places. This is why powers of ten make unit conversions so easy: 0.045 metres × 100 = 4.5 centimetres, and 0.045 metres × 1000 = 45 millimetres, because there are 100 centimetres and 1000 millimetres in a metre.
concepts.example: Here is a real example. If a small sweet costs $0.12 and Khadija buys 100 of them, the total is 0.12 × 100 = $12.00. The digits 1 and 2 moved two places to the left, making the number one hundred times bigger. Working backwards uses division: if 100 sweets cost $12, then one sweet costs 12 ÷ 100 = $0.12.

concepts.title: Rounding Decimal Numbers
concepts.explanation:
Rounding replaces a number with a nearby, simpler number that is easier to say and work with. It is easier to report that “Usain Bolt ran 100 metres in under 10 seconds” than to quote his exact time of 9.63 seconds. We round all the time – for money, measurements and estimates.

The method is always the same. First, decide which place you are rounding to. Then look at the very next digit to its right. If that next digit is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4, you round down (leave the rounding digit unchanged). If it is 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9, you round up (increase the rounding digit by 1). Then drop everything after the rounding place.

Rounding to the nearest tenth – look at the hundredths digit:

8.84 → hundredths digit is 4 → round down → 8.8.

6.47 → hundredths digit is 7 → round up → 6.5.

3.95 → hundredths digit is 5 → round up → the 9 tenths becomes 10 tenths, which carries: 4.0.

That last example, 3.95, shows a tricky case worth studying. Rounding the 9 up makes it 10, which is a full extra whole, so it carries over just like in addition, giving 4.0. Do not panic when a 9 rounds up – simply carry it, exactly as you would when adding.

Rounding to the nearest whole number – look at the tenths digit:

4.09 → tenths digit is 0 → round down → 4.

7.89 → tenths digit is 8 → round up → 8.

2.5 → tenths digit is 5 → round up → 3.

The same method rounds to the nearest hundredth (look at the thousandths digit) or nearest thousandth (look at the next digit along). For instance, 8.2749 to the nearest hundredth: the thousandths digit is 4, so round down to 8.27. To the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit 7, so round up to 8.3. The rule never changes – only the place you focus on changes.
concepts.example: ⭐ Common Slip to Avoid Always look at the ONE digit immediately to the right of your rounding place – not any further along. For the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit. For the nearest whole, look at the tenths digit.

concepts.title: The History of Our Number System
concepts.explanation: The place-value system you use every day, where the same ten digits (0-9) can represent any number no matter how large, was not always how people counted. Ancient Egyptians used separate hieroglyph symbols for 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 and simply repeated them, so writing 999 needed 27 symbols. The Romans used letters like I, V, X, L, C, D and M, and their system had no symbol for zero at all and no place value — the position of a digit did not change its meaning, so calculations like long multiplication were extremely difficult with it. The breakthrough came in India, roughly 1,500 years ago, where mathematicians invented a system with exactly ten digits, including a symbol for zero, and gave each position in a number ten times the value of the position to its right. This is called a place-value or positional system, and it is the same system used worldwide today. The idea travelled from India to the Arab world, where scholars refined and spread it further across trade routes into Europe, which is why it is now called the Hindu-Arabic numeral system. Zero was the true breakthrough: without a symbol for 'nothing in this place', you cannot tell 5 from 50 from 500 just by writing '5'. Zero acts as a placeholder that holds a position open, and it also lets us represent the number 'nothing' itself. Today's system is powerful because only ten symbols and one idea — place value — can represent any number, however large or small, and support fast written calculation methods like the ones you use throughout this unit.
concepts.example: Try writing the number 2,406 in Roman numerals: MMCDVI. Notice there is no way to show that the '4' in 406 means 'four hundred' just from its position — every value needs its own symbols, and there is no zero at all. Now write 2,406 in our place-value system: the digit 2 is worth 2,000 because of where it sits, the 4 is worth 400, the 0 holds the tens place empty, and the 6 is worth 6 units. Changing only the position of the digit 4 — for example writing 2,046 instead of 2,406 — completely changes its value from 400 to 40, without changing the digit itself. That is the power of place value that the Hindu-Arabic system gave the world.

concepts.title: Estimating Position on a Number Line
concepts.explanation: A number line shows numbers in order along a straight line, but it does not always have every mark labelled. Often you are given only the two end points — for example a line starting at 0 and ending at 10,000 — and asked to judge roughly where another number, like 6,300, should go. To estimate a position, first work out what fraction or proportion of the way along the line your number is. Since 6,300 is a little more than halfway between 0 and 10,000 (halfway would be 5,000), you would mark it a little past the midpoint. A useful strategy is to mentally divide the line into easy benchmark sections — halves, then quarters, then tenths — and compare your number with each benchmark until you can picture roughly where it belongs. This skill matters because in real life, scales are rarely marked at every single value: thermometers, rulers, jars and gauges often show only a few marked points, and you must judge the rest by proportion.
concepts.example: Estimate the position of 8,750 on a number line from 0 to 10,000. Halfway is 5,000, and three-quarters of the way is 7,500. Since 8,750 = 7/8 × 10,000, it sits clearly past the three-quarter mark and close to the right-hand end, roughly seven-eighths of the way along the line.

methods.title: How to compare two decimals
steps: Give both numbers the same number of decimal places by adding zeros.
Compare the whole-number parts first.
If equal, compare the tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.
Write the correct symbol: >, < or =.

methods.title: How to multiply or divide by a power of ten
steps: Count the zeros in 10, 100 or 1000 — that is how many places to move.
Multiplying moves the digits left; dividing moves them right.
Fill any empty places with zeros as placeholders.

methods.title: How to round a decimal
steps: Decide which place you are rounding to.
Look at the single digit immediately to its right.
Round up if it is 5 or more, down if it is 4 or less.
Drop everything after the rounding place (and carry if a 9 rounds up).

methods.title: Ordering decimals
steps: Rewrite each with three decimal places: 0.670, 0.607, 0.700, 0.067.
Compare place by place.
The order from smallest is 0.067 < 0.607 < 0.67 < 0.7.
Adding the zeros made the comparison easy.

methods.title: A chain of powers of ten
methods.example: Follow the number: start with 0.6, then ×10, then ×100, then ÷1000.
steps: So the chain is 0.6 → 6 → 600 → 0.6.
Interestingly, it returns to where it began, because ×10 ×100 = ×1000, which the final ÷1000 undoes.

methods.title: Rounding to the nearest hundredth
steps: The hundredths digit is 4.
Look at the next digit to the right, the thousandths digit, which is 7.
Since 7 is 5 or more, round the hundredths up from 4 to 5.
The answer is 15.85.

workedExamples.title: The value of a digit
workedExamples.prompt: What is the value of the digit 5 in the number 12.357?
workedExamples.solution: Read the places after the point: 3 is tenths, 5 is hundredths, 7 is thousandths. So the 5 sits in the hundredths place and is worth 0.05 (five hundredths). A common wrong answer is “thousandths,” but the 7 — not the 5 — is in the thousandths place.

workedExamples.title: Words into a number
workedExamples.prompt: Write “seven and twenty-four thousandths” in figures.
workedExamples.solution: The word “and” marks the decimal point, so the whole part is 7. “Twenty-four thousandths” must end in the thousandths column: 24 written across the last three places is 0-2-4. So the answer is 7.024. The zero in the tenths place is essential.

workedExamples.title: Expanded form
workedExamples.solution: 8 ones, 1 tenth, 4 hundredths, 6 thousandths, giving 8 + 0.1 + 0.04 + 0.006. Check by adding the parts: 8 + 0.1 + 0.04 + 0.006 = 8.146. It matches.

workedExamples.title: Ordering decimals
workedExamples.solution: Rewrite each with three decimal places: 0.670, 0.607, 0.700, 0.067. Compare place by place. The order from smallest is 0.067 < 0.607 < 0.67 < 0.7. Adding the zeros made the comparison easy.

workedExamples.title: A chain of powers of ten
workedExamples.prompt: Follow the number: start with 0.6, then ×10, then ×100, then ÷1000.
workedExamples.solution: 0.6 × 10 = 6; 6 × 100 = 600; 600 ÷ 1000 = 0.6. So the chain is 0.6 → 6 → 600 → 0.6. Interestingly, it returns to where it began, because ×10 ×100 = ×1000, which the final ÷1000 undoes.

workedExamples.title: Rounding to the nearest hundredth
workedExamples.solution: The hundredths digit is 4. Look at the next digit to the right, the thousandths digit, which is 7. Since 7 is 5 or more, round the hundredths up from 4 to 5. The answer is 15.85.

workedExamples.title: A scaling word problem
workedExamples.prompt: A recipe needs 3.75 kg of flour for 10 people. How much is needed for 100 people?
workedExamples.solution: 100 people is 10 times as many as 10 people, so we need 10 times as much flour: 3.75 × 10 = 37.5 kg. The digits moved one place to the left.

workedExamples.title: Comparing temperatures
workedExamples.prompt: One morning a fridge reads −3°C and a freezer reads −18°C. Which is colder, and by how much?
workedExamples.solution: On the number line −18 is further to the left than −3, so the freezer is colder. The difference is the number of steps between them: from −18 up to −3 is 15 steps, so the freezer is 15 degrees colder.

workedExamples.title: Rounding to different places
workedExamples.prompt: Round 8.2749 to: a) nearest thousandth b) nearest hundredth c) nearest tenth d) nearest whole number.

workedExamples.title: Converting metres to centimetres and millimetres
workedExamples.prompt: Express 0.045 metres in a) centimetres (×100) b) millimetres (×1000).

workedExamples.title: Ordering temperatures
workedExamples.prompt: Put these temperatures in order from coldest to warmest: 4°C, −2°C, −7°C, 0°C, 3°C.

activities.title: Decimal Detective
steps: Be a Decimal Detective and decode mysterious numbers. For each number, write the value of every digit.
Take the number 4.237. Write: the 4 is ___ ones, the 2 is ___ tenths, the 3 is ___ hundredths, the 7 is ___ thousandths.
Now say the whole number in words two different ways.
Do the same detective report for 15.068 and 0.405.
Challenge: make a decimal where the thousandths digit is larger than the tenths digit, and decode it.

activities.title: Build a Place Value Grid with Coins
activities.materials: small objects to stand for ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths (for example large stones, bottle caps, beans and seeds).
steps: Draw a grid with columns: Ones, point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Ask a family member, or your AI tutor, to call out a decimal such as 3.456.
Place the right number of objects in each column to build it.
Say the number aloud, then decompose it: 3 + 0.4 + 0.05 + 0.006.

activities.title: The Power of Ten Race Track
steps: Draw a race track with checkpoints. A starting number races round, and at each checkpoint it is multiplied or divided by a power of ten.
Racer 1 starts at 3.45: ×10, then ×100, then ÷10. Write the number after each checkpoint.
Racer 2 starts at 67: ×1000, then ÷100, then ×10.
Racer 3 starts at 0.8: ×100, then ×10, then ÷1000.
Design your own race for 2.5 with four checkpoints and give it to a friend, or your AI tutor, to solve.

activities.title: Rounding Restaurant
steps: You own a restaurant, and every price must be rounded for different purposes – some to the nearest whole shilling, some to the nearest ten cents.
Butterfly Burger costs 8.67. Round it to the nearest whole and to the nearest tenth.
Place Value Pasta costs 15.89. Round it both ways.
The freezer reads −18.7°C. Round it to the nearest whole degree.
Invent three more menu prices and round each one two ways.

activities.title: Real-World Number Hunt (Family Task)
activities.materials: your home, and any prices, labels or measurements you can find.
steps: Hunt for ten decimal numbers around the house – on packets, rulers, scales or bills.
For each one, write where you found it and what each digit is worth.
Choose five and explain when someone might round them and why.
Pick one measurement and show what happens when you multiply it by 10 and by 100.

activities.title: Number Line Temperatures (Investigation)
steps: Draw a number line from −10 to 10 with zero in the middle.
Mark these temperatures on it: −7, −2, 0, 3, 8.
Over one day, record the temperature in the early morning and at midday, and mark both.
Work out how many degrees the temperature rose between your two readings.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand decimals best? Which concept – place value, powers of ten, rounding or negatives – do you feel most confident about now? What was the trickiest part, and what would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Place Value Rule
rules.text: Each place to the left is ten times bigger; each place to the right is ten times smaller. Places after the point: tenths (0.1), hundredths (0.01), thousandths (0.001). In 13.136: 1 ten, 3 ones, 1 tenth, 3 hundredths, 6 thousandths.

rules.title: Powers of Ten Rule
rules.text: Multiply by 10, 100, 1000 = digits move Left = number gets Larger. Divide by 10, 100, 1000 = digits move Right = number gets smaller. The number of zeros tells you how many places to move.

rules.title: Rounding Rule
rules.text: Look at the one digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 round down; 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 round up. Nearest tenth: look at hundredths. Nearest whole: look at tenths.

rules.title: Negative Numbers Rule
rules.text: Numbers left of zero are negative and get smaller as you move further left. Negative 5 is smaller and colder than negative 2.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A number multiplied by 100 gives 456.7. What is the original number?
A number rounds to 12 to the nearest whole number and rounds to 11.8 to the nearest tenth. Give one number it could be.
The factory records masses 2.345, 2.354, 2.435, 2.453, 2.534, 2.543 kg. Rounded to the nearest hundredth, how many different values are there?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The rounded values are 2.35, 2.35, 2.44, 2.45, 2.53, 2.54, giving 5 different values.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Find a decimal with three decimal places that, multiplied by 1000, gives a whole number, rounds to 7.3 to the nearest tenth, and whose digits add to 15.
Explain the key idea in Rounding Decimal Numbers.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Rounding replaces a number with a nearby, simpler number that is easier to say and work with. It is easier to report that “Usain Bolt ran 100 metres in under 10 seconds” than to quote his exact time of 9.63 seconds. We round all the time – for money, measurements and estimates. The method is always the same. First, decide which place you are rounding to. Then look at the very next digit to its right. If that next digit is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4, you round down (leave the rounding digit unchanged). If it is 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9, you round up (increase the rounding digit by one).

selfAssessment: I can read, write and understand whole numbers up to the millions, and decimals with up to three decimal places (tenths, hundredths, thousandths).
I can explain the value of each digit in a number using its place.
I can compose numbers by combining place value parts, and decompose numbers into their parts.
I can regroup a decimal in different ways while keeping the same value.
I can compare and order decimal numbers using place value.
I can multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000, explaining how the digits move.
I can round decimals to the nearest whole number, tenth, hundredth or thousandth.
I can read and order negative numbers on a number line and in real contexts such as temperature.
I can use estimation to check that answers are sensible, and apply these skills to money, measurement and science problems.
